text:
IDEA: Develop biomimetic nanoparticle carriers functionalized with dual brain-targeting ligands that selectively engage receptor-mediated transcytosis pathways to achieve efficient BBB crossing while incorporating anti-inflammatory surface modifications to minimize neuroinflammation and preserve neural function.

BACKGROUND: Efficient drug delivery across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) remains a critical bottleneck in treating central nervous system disorders due to the barrier’s restrictive nature and potential adverse neural effects. Existing targeted delivery systems mainly focus on maximizing transport efficiency but often overlook the resultant neuroinflammatory responses and long-term neural safety, limiting their clinical translation.

APPROACH: Engineer biomimetic nanoparticles coated with ligands for combined targeting of transferrin and insulin receptors to leverage multiple receptor-mediated transcytosis routes for enhanced BBB penetration. Simultaneously, incorporate surface-bound anti-inflammatory peptides (e.g., Annexin A1 mimetics) to suppress microglial activation and astrocyte-mediated neuroinflammation. Validate carrier integrity and receptor engagement using in vitro human BBB models based on iPSC-derived brain microvascular endothelial cells co-cultured with astrocytes and pericytes.

EXPERIMENT: Evaluate transcytosis efficiency via quantitative fluorescence and mass spectrometry of cargo delivery in the in vitro BBB model and in vivo in murine models using established brain biodistribution assays. Assess neuroinflammatory markers (IL-1β, TNF-α), microglial activation states (Iba1 staining), and electrophysiological neural function tests post-administration to measure neural safety.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing primarily on BBB penetration or drug load, this approach uniquely integrates dual-receptor targeting to maximize delivery efficiency with an explicit design element for neural safety by mitigating neuroinflammation, addressing a critical translational barrier unexamined in previous biomimetic carrier studies.

IDEA: Develop enzyme-responsive oral drug delivery systems that release therapeutics selectively in intestinal regions by triggering payload release in response to specific gut enzymes, enabling precise site-specific drug targeting beyond pH-dependent mechanisms.

BACKGROUND: Conventional oral drug delivery systems often rely on pH changes to trigger drug release, which can be imprecise due to variable gastrointestinal pH and result in off-target release and reduced therapeutic efficacy. Additionally, current formulations lack the ability to respond to biological signals intrinsic to gut environments, such as enzymatic activity, which varies spatially along the gastrointestinal tract. Addressing this limitation is critical to improving site-specific delivery for diseases localized in distinct gut segments.

APPROACH: Design polymeric or nanoparticle-based drug carriers functionalized with enzyme-cleavable linkers or coatings that respond specifically to intestinal enzymes such as pancreatic proteases (e.g., trypsin, chymotrypsin) or brush-border enzymes (e.g., alkaline phosphatase). These carriers will remain stable in acidic stomach conditions and release their payload only upon exposure to target enzymes in the small intestine or colon. Characterization will involve in vitro enzymatic degradation assays and drug release profiles using simulated gastrointestinal fluids with relevant enzymes, followed by in vivo oral administration in rodent models to evaluate site-specificity through imaging of labeled carriers and pharmacokinetics.

EXPERIMENT: Test enzyme-triggered release kinetics using established in vitro simulated gastric and intestinal fluids with and without target enzymes; evaluate site-specific accumulation and therapeutic efficacy in animal models of intestinal disease (e.g., inflammatory bowel disease mouse model) by quantifying drug concentration along gut segments using fluorescence or radiolabel tracking and measuring therapeutic outcomes such as inflammation markers. Metrics include cumulative release percentage, enzyme-specific release rate, bioavailability, and disease biomarker reduction.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior oral delivery systems relying mainly on pH or passive diffusion triggers, this approach leverages biologically relevant enzymatic cues unique to gut microenvironments for highly specific, controlled drug release, minimizing premature release and enhancing therapeutic precision. This enzyme-responsive mechanism offers a biologically intrinsic, modular targeting strategy that overcomes limitations of existing pH-dependent or nonspecific oral carriers.

IDEA: Develop microneedle arrays with mechanically tunable penetration depth enabling personalized transdermal drug delivery tailored to individual skin properties and targeted dermal layers.

BACKGROUND: Conventional microneedle patches have fixed needle lengths that do not account for variability in skin thickness and mechanical properties across patients, which can lead to suboptimal drug delivery depth and inconsistent therapeutic outcomes. Personalized adjustment of penetration depth is critical to precisely target specific skin layers for enhanced efficacy and reduced adverse effects.

APPROACH: Design and fabricate microneedle patches incorporating an embedded mechanical adjustment mechanism—such as a micro-screw or shape-memory element—that allows on-demand tuning of needle length immediately before or during application. Characterize the adjustable penetration depth through mechanical force sensors and validate consistent drug release profiles using model compounds loaded in the needles.

EXPERIMENT: Perform ex vivo penetration force tests on human skin samples from donors of varied age, ethnicity, and anatomical sites to measure insertion depth and tissue targeting accuracy under different needle length settings; quantify localized drug deposition via fluorescence imaging of a model drug and assess release kinetics in vitro.

NOVELTY: Unlike existing fixed-length or pre-set microneedle designs, this system provides dynamic, user-controlled modulation of needle penetration enabling truly personalized transdermal delivery; integration of mechanical tunability directly into the patch is novel, facilitating adaptation to patient-specific skin variability and therapeutic needs without requiring multiple patch versions.

IDEA: Develop biosensor-integrated nanoparticle drug carriers that dynamically adjust antibody-drug release rates in response to real-time autoimmune disease biomarkers, enabling adaptive immunotherapy aligned with fluctuating disease activity.

BACKGROUND: Autoimmune diseases often exhibit unpredictable flare and remission cycles, but current antibody-drug delivery systems typically provide static release profiles that fail to adapt to these fluctuations, leading to suboptimal therapeutic efficacy and increased side effects. There is a critical need for smart delivery platforms capable of modulating drug release in response to dynamic changes in disease biomarkers or local inflammatory signals to improve treatment precision.

APPROACH: Engineer polymeric nanoparticles embedded with molecular biosensors sensitive to key autoimmune biomarkers—such as pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) or reactive oxygen species—that trigger conformational or chemical changes to modulate antibody-drug release kinetics in situ. The system will couple a feedback-responsive mechanism where elevated biomarker levels induce accelerated release during flares, while minimal release occurs during remission. Drug release profiles will be fine-tuned via nanoparticle surface chemistry and biosensor design to enable rapid, reversible response to biomarker concentration changes.

EXPERIMENT: Evaluate the system using an established murine model of rheumatoid arthritis, quantifying in vivo release kinetics of therapeutic antibody drugs correlated to serial measurements of inflammatory cytokine levels via ELISA and biosensor readouts. Therapeutic efficacy will be compared against static-release nanoparticle controls using clinical arthritis scoring, histopathology, and pro-inflammatory biomarker reduction as primary metrics.

NOVELTY: Unlike existing nanocarriers with fixed-release profiles, this approach integrates biosensing elements within the delivery platform to dynamically synchronize antibody-drug administration with fluctuating autoimmune disease activity, offering a precision immunoengineering strategy that adapts therapy in real-time to improve efficacy and minimize adverse effects.

text:
IDEA: Develop dual-ligand nanoparticle-antibody conjugates capable of selectively targeting and delivering immunomodulatory drugs to activation-state-specific dispersed pathogenic immune cell subsets in systemic autoimmune diseases while minimizing off-target immune activation.

BACKGROUND: Current immunoengineering strategies for autoimmune disorders often suffer from nonspecific targeting of immune cells, leading to widespread immune activation and associated toxicities. There is a critical need for delivery systems that can discriminate immune cells not only by surface markers but also by their activation state to avoid bystander effects and improve treatment efficacy.

APPROACH: Engineer polymeric nanoparticles conjugated with dual recognition ligands—one antibody specific to a pathogenic immune cell subset and a second ligand that senses the activation state via an activation-induced surface marker or conformational epitope. These nanoparticles will incorporate on-demand drug release mechanisms triggered by the activation state (e.g., enzymatic cleavage or pH changes specific to activated cells), ensuring selective delivery of immunomodulatory payloads. The system will be optimized to minimize uptake by resting immune cells and maximize targeting of dispersed pathogenic cells.

EXPERIMENT: Validate selective targeting and activation-dependent drug release using in vitro co-cultures of activated and resting immune cells from human autoimmune patient PBMC samples, measuring cell-specific uptake, activation markers, and cytokine profiles. In vivo efficacy and safety will be evaluated in established systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) mouse models using biodistribution imaging, flow cytometry of immune subsets, disease activity scores (e.g., proteinuria, autoantibody titers), and histopathology.

NOVELTY: This approach uniquely integrates dual-ligand targeting with activation-state sensing and triggered drug release, surpassing conventional single-ligand or nonspecific delivery systems that cannot discriminate immune cell activation states, thereby significantly reducing off-target effects and improving therapeutic precision in systemic autoimmune diseases.

IDEA: Engineer antibody-displaying immune cells with integrated synthetic feedback circuits that dynamically adjust activation thresholds in response to inflammatory signals to maintain persistent viral targeting while preventing immunopathology during chronic infections.

BACKGROUND: Chronic viral infections often provoke uncontrolled immune activation leading to tissue damage and immunopathology, as current therapeutic antibody or cell-based approaches lack mechanisms for dynamic immune modulation. Sustained antiviral activity requires balancing effective viral control with immune regulation, which remains an unmet challenge in immunoengineering for therapeutic use of antibody drugs.

APPROACH: Develop immune cells engineered to display therapeutic antibodies on their surface coupled with synthetic gene circuits that sense local inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α) and adjust their activation or effector functions accordingly by modulating intracellular signaling thresholds. This dynamic feedback control aims to sustain antiviral activity while minimizing systemic inflammation, implemented using inducible promoters and receptor-based biosensors integrated with antibody expression systems.

EXPERIMENT: Validate in established chronic viral infection mouse models (e.g., LCMV clone 13) by assessing systemic cytokine profiles, viral load kinetics, immune cell activation states, and histopathological examination of tissues. Compare against baseline models using constitutively active antibody-expressing immune cells and checkpoint inhibitor treatments, evaluating efficacy via viral suppression and safety via markers of immunopathology.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior static antibody or cell therapies, this approach incorporates real-time, feedback-mediated immune regulation engineered at the cellular level to dynamically balance antiviral efficacy with immune tolerance, preventing tissue damage while maintaining persistent targeting—a key advancement in immunoengineered antibody therapeutics.

topic: iPSC derived cardiomyocytes on a chip
text:
IDEA: Develop and validate an integrated microfluidic platform with optimized cell culture and automated multiplexed electrophysiological recording protocols to enable rapid 48-hour turnaround pharmacological testing of iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte-neuron co-cultures.

BACKGROUND: Current heart-on-a-chip models incorporating iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and neurons provide valuable insights into cardiac function and neuro-cardiac interactions but suffer from long assay times and cumbersome manual handling, limiting their utility for rapid drug screening. There is a critical need for streamlined protocols that minimize culture and dosing preparation time while maintaining physiological relevance and signal fidelity for acute pharmacological testing.

APPROACH: Design a microfluidic device integrating co-cultures of iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and autonomic neurons with automated fluid handling for sequential drug dosing and washout, combined with on-chip multiplexed electrophysiological sensors (e.g., multi-electrode arrays and impedance sensors). Develop standardized culture and dosing protocols optimized for cell maturation and rapid drug response within 48 hours. Implement software for automated signal acquisition and noise reduction to enable high-throughput, real-time electrophysiological monitoring.

EXPERIMENT: Validate the system using a panel of well-characterized fast-acting cardiac (e.g., dofetilide, verapamil) and neuroactive drugs (e.g., isoproterenol, propranolol) by comparing electrophysiological parameters such as action potential duration, beat rate variability, and conduction velocity against conventional longer-term culture assays. Assess reproducibility (coefficient of variation), throughput (number of assays per week), and sensitivity (drug concentration-response curves) to demonstrate rapid assay turnaround and reliability.

NOVELTY: This work combines hardware innovation and optimized biological protocols into an integrated workflow explicitly designed for rapid, multiplexed neuro-cardiac pharmacology testing within 48 hours, significantly reducing assay time and manual labor compared to existing heart-on-a-chip models that predominantly focus on long-term culture and single-cell type assays.

text:
IDEA: Develop a flexible, modular microfluidic heart-on-a-chip platform optimized for patient-specific iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes that supports robust functional assays from fewer than 10,000 cells by enabling customizable chip geometry and co-culture conditions.

BACKGROUND: Existing iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte (iPSC-CM) heart-on-a-chip systems generally require large cell inputs and fixed chip formats, limiting their applicability for patient-specific studies where cell yield and differentiation efficiency are often low and variable. This bottleneck restricts personalized drug screening and functional modeling particularly for rare patient samples or limited biopsy material. Addressing this challenge demands adaptable platforms that maintain physiological relevance despite low cell numbers.

APPROACH: Design a modular microfluidic platform with adjustable chamber sizes and interchangeable co-culture modules (e.g., endothelial cells, fibroblasts, neurons) that can be tailored based on available cell input and desired microenvironment complexity. Integrate real-time functional readouts such as contractility, calcium transient imaging, and electrophysiology via embedded sensors to assess cardiac physiology with minimal cell numbers. Validate system performance and patient specificity using iPSC-CMs derived from multiple patients with varied differentiation efficiencies.

EXPERIMENT: Employ iPSC-CMs from at least three patients with known genetic backgrounds and differentiate them with varying yields to seed the custom chips with fewer than 10,000 cells each. Measure functional parameters including beating frequency, contractile force via flexible strain gauges, and drug response profiles to standard cardioactive compounds (e.g., isoproterenol, doxorubicin). Compare data against conventional fixed-format heart-on-a-chip platforms seeded with higher cell numbers to benchmark sensitivity and reproducibility.

NOVELTY: This approach uniquely addresses the critical limitation of input cell quantity by enabling low-cell-number assays customizable to patient sample variability, whereas prior platforms rely on large, fixed-format cultures. The modular design permits flexible co-culture inclusion and real-time functional integration, expanding the translational potential for personalized cardiac disease modeling and drug screening.

text:
IDEA: Develop a microfluidic heart-on-a-chip platform integrating iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and sympathetic neurons optimized for rapid (<24 hour) electrophysiological and calcium imaging assays to evaluate acute neuro-cardiac drug toxicity with high sensitivity and reproducibility.

BACKGROUND: Current heart-on-a-chip models incorporating iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and neuronal components enable studies of chronic neuro-cardiac interactions but typically require multi-day culture times and complex multicellular co-cultures, limiting their utility for rapid drug screening. There is a critical need for streamlined, fast-turnaround assays that capture acute neuro-cardiac electrophysiological responses to candidate drugs, enabling faster and more predictive cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity assessment.

APPROACH: We will engineer a simplified microfluidic chip architecture supporting co-culture of human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and sympathetic neurons with optimized microenvironment cues to promote rapid functional neuro-cardiac coupling within hours of plating. High-sensitivity multielectrode arrays (MEAs) coupled with real-time calcium imaging will be employed to monitor electrophysiological and calcium transient changes induced by acute drug exposure within 24 hours. The system will minimize culture complexity by excluding fibroblasts and endothelial layers while preserving essential neuro-cardiac signaling features.

EXPERIMENT: Validation will involve testing a panel of well-characterized acute cardiotoxic and neurotoxic drugs (e.g., isoproterenol, doxorubicin, propranolol, and nicotine) measuring electrophysiological parameters (beat rate, conduction velocity, arrhythmic events) and calcium transient kinetics before and after <24-hour drug application. Sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility will be benchmarked against extended-duration co-culture models from literature and standard patch-clamp or calcium imaging datasets.

NOVELTY: This approach uniquely balances minimal culture complexity and ultra-rapid assay time to enable acute neuro-cardiac functional assessment, unlike existing models requiring days for maturation and long-term drug exposure. It prioritizes speed and throughput for early-stage drug triage while maintaining physiologically relevant neuro-cardiac interactions previously unachieved in short-term assays.

IDEA: Develop a nanodisc-based antigen mimetic platform to present native membrane protein conformations for phage and yeast display antibody selection, enhancing the discovery of antibodies targeting conformational epitopes on membrane proteins.

BACKGROUND: Antigen-specific antibody discovery against membrane proteins is challenging due to instability and misfolding when proteins are detergent-solubilized or presented in denatured forms, resulting in loss of native epitopes. Current screening methods often fail to capture antibodies binding conformation-dependent or membrane-proximal epitopes essential for therapeutic and diagnostic targeting.

APPROACH: We propose to incorporate purified membrane proteins into lipid nanodiscs, stabilizing their native conformation embedded in a lipid bilayer, and use these nanodisc-antigen complexes as soluble antigens in phage and yeast display selections. The approach balances nanodisc biochemical accessibility with stability to improve selection stringency and fidelity. Binding affinity and epitope specificity will be assessed by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and competition assays against detergent-solubilized antigens to confirm enhanced native epitope presentation.

EXPERIMENT: Antibody discovery campaigns targeting clinically relevant membrane proteins (e.g., MuSK or AChR involved in myasthenia gravis) will compare selections using nanodisc-incorporated antigens versus detergent-solubilized controls. Metrics include the affinity (KD) measured by SPR, epitope mapping via alanine scanning mutagenesis, and functional neutralization assays where applicable.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior methods relying on detergent or denatured antigen presentations, this platform uses nanodiscs to maintain native membrane protein conformation in a soluble format compatible with display technologies, enabling the discovery of antibodies against challenging conformational and membrane-proximal epitopes that have been underexplored in antibody discovery.

IDEA: Develop a high-purity isolation method for rare autoreactive B cells from autoimmune patient samples using advanced multi-parameter flow cytometry with novel marker panels and optimized gating strategies that overcome immune dysregulation and noisy self-reactivity signals.

BACKGROUND: Current antigen-specific antibody discovery methods often struggle to isolate extremely rare pathogenic autoreactive B cells from heterogeneous autoimmune samples due to low frequency, background self-reactivity, and immune dysregulation, limiting sensitivity and purity. Standard antigen baiting approaches have insufficient specificity and throughput, hindering downstream characterization and therapeutic antibody development.

APPROACH: We propose leveraging multi-parameter flow cytometry integrating novel combinatorial surface and intracellular markers indicative of autoreactivity and immune activation states, combined with refined gating algorithms that dynamically adjust for patient-specific immune profiles. This method will enable precise sorting of autoreactive B cells at much higher purity and throughput than classical antigen baiting. Post-sort validation will employ single-cell BCR sequencing and functional assays to confirm pathogenic specificity.

EXPERIMENT: The technique will be evaluated on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from well-characterized cohorts of myasthenia gravis patients, including seronegative cases, benchmarked against conventional antigen baiting and single-parameter sorting. Metrics will include purity of sorted cells (validated by BCR clonality and antigen reactivity), throughput, and enrichment fold change of autoreactive clones.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior methods focused on antigen baiting alone, this approach integrates multi-dimensional immune marker profiling with adaptive gating to isolate rare autoreactive B cells with unprecedented purity and scalability, directly addressing immune heterogeneity and dysregulation in autoimmune disease samples.

IDEA: Develop a transfer learning framework that leverages large-scale antibody-antigen interaction datasets to generate de novo antibody sequences specifically targeting rare and emerging pathogens with limited available data.

BACKGROUND: Antibody discovery against rare or newly emerging pathogens is hampered by the scarcity of sequence and structural information, limiting conventional homology modeling and high-throughput screening approaches. Current antibody design methods often require abundant target-specific data, which is unavailable during emergent outbreaks, delaying therapeutic and diagnostic development.

APPROACH: Utilize pretrained deep learning models trained on massive antibody-antigen binding datasets such as the Observed Antibody Space (OAS) and SAbDab structural database, then fine-tune these models using limited sequence or epitope data from emerging pathogens. The framework will generate candidate antibody sequences optimized for binding specificity through sequence-to-affinity prediction and structural plausibility scoring, incorporating simulation-based validation (e.g., molecular dynamics or docking).

EXPERIMENT: Validate the approach retrospectively on recent emerging pathogens like SARS-CoV-2 and Nipah virus by training on pre-pandemic antibody datasets and testing design performance on pandemic-specific antibodies. Metrics include binding affinity prediction accuracy (e.g., ROC-AUC), sequence novelty and diversity, and in silico binding stability scores compared against baseline methods like standard phage display-derived antibodies or homology-based modeling.

NOVELTY: This approach uniquely applies transfer learning from large, general antibody-antigen interaction data to the challenge of rare pathogen antibody design, addressing data scarcity in emergent situations. Unlike conventional methods that rely on target-specific experimental data, this method enables rapid in silico generation and prioritization of antibodies, accelerating therapeutic candidate discovery in outbreak scenarios.

topic_id: CUSTOM:mandibular bone regeneration using tissue engineering
topic: Mandibular bone regeneration using tissue engineering
text:
IDEA: Develop enzyme-responsive immunomodulatory scaffolds that detect elevated matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity in chronically inflamed mandibular bone defects to dynamically release immunomodulators and promote bone regeneration by actively controlling the inflammatory microenvironment.

BACKGROUND: Chronic inflammation in mandibular bone defects impairs bone regeneration by disrupting the healing cascade and creating a hostile microenvironment. Current scaffolds for mandibular regeneration mainly provide static release of osteogenic factors without adapting to the fluctuating inflammatory status, leading to suboptimal outcomes in chronic conditions. There is a pressing need for biomaterials that can sense biochemical cues indicative of inflammation and respond by modulating immune responses to favor tissue repair.

APPROACH: We propose to design a 3D-printed composite scaffold embedded with enzyme-cleavable linkers responsive to elevated MMPs common in chronic inflammation. These linkers will tether immunomodulatory agents (e.g., IL-10 or resolvin analogs) that are released in response to high local MMP activity. The scaffold will also incorporate osteoconductive components such as PCL/β-TCP for structural support and bone regeneration. In vitro, enzyme-triggered release profiles and immunomodulatory effects on macrophage polarization will be assessed, followed by in vivo evaluation in a rabbit mandibular critical-sized defect model with induced chronic inflammation.

EXPERIMENT: Test enzyme-responsive release kinetics using fluorescence-labeled immunomodulators in simulated MMP-rich environments; evaluate macrophage phenotype shifts (M1/M2 markers) in co-culture assays; assess bone regeneration via micro-CT and histomorphometry at 4, 8, and 12 weeks post-implantation in chronic inflammation and normal groups. Metrics include MMP-triggered release rate, inflammatory cytokine levels, bone volume/total volume (BV/TV), and biomechanical strength.

NOVELTY: This strategy is the first to incorporate an active biochemical sensing mechanism into mandibular bone scaffolds that dynamically modulate immune responses based on local enzyme activity, providing a responsive alternative to static delivery systems; it integrates immunomodulation with enzyme-triggered drug release specifically targeted to the biochemical environment of chronic mandibular inflammation.

topic_id: CUSTOM:mandibular bone regeneration using tissue engineering
topic: Mandibular bone regeneration using tissue engineering
text:
IDEA: Develop gradient 3D bioprinted scaffolds with spatially varying stiffness and porosity that provide central mechanical support and peripheral enhanced nutrient diffusion to optimize large segmental mandibular bone regeneration.

BACKGROUND: Large segmental mandibular defects require scaffolds that can withstand significant masticatory forces while also allowing for timely vascularization and nutrient delivery to support cell viability and bone regeneration. Existing uniform scaffolds often fail to balance mechanical strength and nutrient diffusion, leading to compromised regeneration or scaffold failure. A scaffold with spatially graded properties is needed to address these conflicting requirements simultaneously.

APPROACH: Utilize multi-material 3D bioprinting to fabricate scaffolds combining a stiffer polycaprolactone/beta-tricalcium phosphate (PCL/β-TCP) core for load-bearing and a more porous, hydrogel-based outer region embedded with pro-angiogenic factors to promote early nutrient diffusion and vascular ingrowth. The scaffold design will feature a continuous gradient in stiffness and porosity from center to periphery, optimized via computational modeling. In vitro perfusion bioreactor studies will characterize nutrient diffusion and cell viability, while mechanical compression tests will assess load-bearing capacity.

EXPERIMENT: Mechanical properties will be benchmarked against uniform PCL/β-TCP scaffolds using standardized compression testing (e.g., ASTM F451). Nutrient diffusion and vascularization potential will be evaluated in vitro using perfusion assays with endothelial and mesenchymal stem cells cultured on scaffolds, measuring oxygen gradients and angiogenic marker expression. Finally, a critical-sized mandibular defect model in rabbits or canines will assess in vivo bone regeneration and scaffold integration over 12 weeks via micro-CT and histology.

NOVELTY: Unlike previous studies employing uniform scaffolds or dual-material composites without spatial gradation, this work integrates continuous gradients of stiffness and porosity tailored precisely to address the mechanical-nutrient diffusion trade-off. The approach enables staged vascularization at the scaffold periphery while preserving core mechanical integrity, a key advancement for functional regeneration in large mandibular defects.

topic: Mandibular bone regeneration using tissue engineering
text:
IDEA: Develop a compartmentalized, multi-material 3D-printed mandibular scaffold with distinct spatial zones enabling temporally controlled sequential release of osteogenic and angiogenic factors to enhance staged bone regeneration and vascularization in large segmental defects.

BACKGROUND: Large mandibular segmental defects require simultaneous regeneration of bone and vasculature to ensure long-term functional recovery, yet existing scaffolds often lack spatial and temporal control of bioactive factor delivery, limiting integration and regeneration efficiency. Current monolithic or dual-factor scaffolds deliver osteogenic and angiogenic signals concurrently or non-specifically, failing to recapitulate the natural sequential process of vascularized bone healing.

APPROACH: Fabricate a multi-phase 3D scaffold using polycaprolactone (PCL)/beta-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP) composite in spatially distinct compartments, incorporating hydrogel microdomains loaded with osteogenic factors (rhBMP-2) in the early zone and angiogenic factors (VEGF) in a delayed-release compartment; utilize biodegradable polymer coatings to temporally modulate release kinetics, enabling an initial osteogenesis phase followed by vascular ingrowth. The scaffold architecture will also be optimized using computational modeling to promote nutrient diffusion and cell infiltration.

EXPERIMENT: Validate in a critical-sized mandibular defect model in rabbits, assessing new bone volume and vascularization using micro-CT, histomorphometry, and immunohistochemical markers at 2, 6, and 10 weeks post-implantation; compare against single-phase scaffolds delivering combined factors and empty defect controls. Quantify mechanical strength restoration using biomechanical testing.

NOVELTY: This study uniquely integrates spatial compartmentalization and temporal release control of osteogenic and angiogenic factors within a single 3D-printed scaffold, mimicking natural healing sequences and overcoming limitations of prior monolithic or simultaneous delivery strategies, thereby improving vascularized bone regeneration in large mandibular defects.

IDEA: Develop a latency-constrained neuro-symbolic embedding update framework that enables real-time robotics control by jointly optimizing symbolic reasoning and sensorimotor representation inference under strict timing budgets.

BACKGROUND: Current neuro-symbolic approaches in robotics often treat symbolic grounding and sensorimotor embedding updates as separate processes, resulting in inference pipelines that are too slow for real-time control loops. This latency bottleneck prevents effective deployment on dynamic robotic tasks requiring rapid perception-action cycles, especially when handling rich streaming multi-modal inputs such as visual, tactile, and proprioceptive data.

APPROACH: We propose a unified neuro-symbolic embedding architecture that integrates continuous sensorimotor embeddings with symbolic reasoning modules, explicitly optimized to minimize both inference and embedding update latency. The method employs a joint training regime with latency-aware loss functions and adaptive update schedules to ensure embedding refreshes meet hard real-time constraints. Symbolic elements will be grounded dynamically through learned mappings to sensorimotor embeddings, enabling fast neuro-symbolic decision-making within physical control loops.

EXPERIMENT: Validation will be conducted on the Meta-World robotic manipulation benchmark (e.g., MT10 and MT50 tasks) with streaming RGB-D and proprioceptive inputs, comparing latency and control accuracy against strong baselines such as classical reinforcement learning policies and recent neuro-symbolic controllers without latency constraints. Metrics include decision latency (ms), task success rate, and closed-loop control stability.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that separately optimizes symbolic reasoning or sensorimotor embeddings without explicit latency guarantees, this framework jointly minimizes inference and update latency under real-time constraints, enabling neuro-symbolic embeddings suitable for time-critical robotic control tasks with multi-modal streaming data.

IDEA: Compliance-focused representation learning for legal texts that integrates symbolic legal knowledge constraints directly into embedding spaces to ensure outputs conform strictly to statutory rules.

BACKGROUND: Current legal representation learning methods often generate embeddings that capture semantic content but fail to guarantee adherence to explicit legal rules and compliance requirements, posing risks in high-stakes applications like automated legal document review or statutory analysis. This gap limits interpretability and the reliability of predictions in regulatory contexts, where strict rule-following is mandatory.

APPROACH: We propose a hybrid representation learning framework that incorporates symbolic legal knowledge—encoded as logic rules or compliance constraints—into the embedding space via constraint-based regularization and explicitly tied symbolic embeddings. The approach jointly trains on large legal corpora such as the EUR-Lex dataset, simultaneously optimizing standard semantic objectives and compliance constraints modeled as differentiable symbolic losses, ensuring learned representations inherently respect legal norms.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on the EUR-Lex and CaseLaw datasets by measuring legal compliance accuracy using designed compliance test suites derived from regulatory statutes, alongside traditional downstream tasks like legal document classification and entailment. Baselines include standard transformer embeddings (e.g., LegalBERT) and graph-based legal representation models, with interpretability assessed through symbolic alignment metrics and rule violation audits.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior representation learning methods that treat legal rules as post-hoc checks or rely solely on implicit learning from text, our method embeds symbolic legal constraints directly into the learning process, enabling inherently compliant, interpretable, and regulation-aware legal representations suitable for real-world high-stakes legal AI systems.

IDEA: Develop hierarchical ontology-aware embeddings that integrate large-scale structured legal ontologies with LLM-generated language embeddings to enhance interpretable and accurate legal document reasoning and precedent retrieval.

BACKGROUND: Current LLM-based legal reasoning methods often rely on opaque, flat vector embeddings that inadequately capture the complex hierarchical structure and semantic relationships inherent in legal ontologies, limiting interpretability and reasoning fidelity. Additionally, legal documents contain multi-level statutory references and precedent dependencies that flat embeddings fail to model explicitly, hindering robust legal inference and retrieval in downstream applications.

APPROACH: We propose a neuro-symbolic framework that jointly learns embeddings of legal texts and their corresponding hierarchical ontology nodes using a graph neural network over the large-scale LEGAL-BERT ontology (or other domain-specific legal ontologies such as LKIF) coupled with LLM contextual embeddings from domain-adapted GPT or LegalBERT. The framework aligns semantic text representations with their positions and relations in the legal ontology hierarchy through multi-level attention mechanisms, enabling explicit hierarchical reasoning. Symbolic logic constraints derived from the ontology guide embedding regularization to preserve interpretability.

EXPERIMENT: Evaluate on publicly available legal reasoning and precedent retrieval benchmarks such as the COLIEE (Competition on Legal Information Extraction/Entailment) dataset and the CaseHOLD dataset, using metrics like F1 score for entailment accuracy and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) for retrieval tasks. Interpretability will be assessed via ontology-conformant explanation fidelity and human expert evaluation of embedding alignment with legal concepts.

NOVELTY: This work meaningfully advances beyond prior black-box or flat embedding approaches by explicitly encoding hierarchical legal ontologies within embeddings, integrating symbolic constraints with LLM representations to improve both reasoning accuracy and interpretability, a combination not previously explored for large-scale legal reasoning tasks.

IDEA:  
Latency-Bounded Dynamic Scheduling (LBDS) dynamically orchestrates asynchronous GPU compute tasks within real-time rendering engines by adaptively redistributing workloads in response to scene complexity fluctuations to guarantee sub-16 ms frame latency without frame drops.

BACKGROUND:  
Real-time rendering engines, especially for interactive applications like games and VR, require strict frame latency bounds (typically 16 ms per frame for 60 FPS). Prior scheduling approaches for asynchronous compute tasks mostly rely on static or heuristic workload partitioning, which fail to adapt to unpredictable scene complexity changes, leading to synchronization stalls or frame drops. Effective dynamic load balancing that anticipates and mitigates these stalls remains an open challenge to maintain smooth frame rates under varying and jittery workloads.

APPROACH:  
LBDS monitors real-time scene complexity metrics and GPU resource utilization within each frame to predict asynchronous compute task loads. It then dynamically reallocates workloads across compute queues and shader cores to balance GPU utilization and avoid costly synchronization points, maintaining frame latency below the 16 ms target. The scheduler employs lightweight machine learning models trained on diverse scene complexity patterns to anticipate workload spikes and preemptively adjust task distribution for minimal frame latency variance.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate LBDS on benchmark real-time engines such as Unreal Engine 5 and Unity using complex, dynamic rendering scenes from datasets like the Sponza Atrium and the NVIDIA Reflex latency benchmarks. Metrics include frame latency distribution, 99th percentile frame time, frame drop rates, GPU utilization, and synchronization stall frequency compared against static scheduling baselines and state-of-the-art heuristics.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior static or heuristic scheduling approaches, LBDS introduces a closed-loop dynamic task redistribution informed by predictive modeling of scene complexity, achieving latency guarantees in unpredictable rendering workloads. This bridging of adaptive scheduling with latency-bounded constraints in asynchronous compute task management is novel in real-time rendering contexts.

IDEA: Develop a power-aware hierarchical temporal sampling framework for time-gated rendering on mobile AR devices that dynamically adapts sampling rates to minimize energy consumption while guaranteeing a target visual quality threshold.

BACKGROUND: Time-gated rendering on resource-constrained mobile AR devices often relies on fixed or heuristic temporal sampling rates, leading to unnecessary energy waste during stable or low-motion scenes. Existing methods overlook dynamic power conditions and sensor input rates, resulting in suboptimal energy-performance trade-offs especially under varying workload and environmental dynamics.

APPROACH: We propose an adaptive temporal sampling strategy that hierarchically selects key frames and intermediate samples based on real-time sensor data variation and device power states. Our method integrates a lightweight power-monitoring module that informs a control algorithm to skip redundant rendering computations during low scene dynamics, maintaining perceptual quality using edge-aware temporal consistency checks. This framework operates within existing time-gated rendering pipelines to achieve an energy-efficient rendering schedule without compromising visual fidelity.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate on publicly available AR video datasets such as the Mobile AR Dataset (MAD) and use real device power profiling on modern AR-capable smartphones (e.g., Google Pixel 7, iPhone 14 Pro). Metrics will include energy consumption reduction (measured via onboard power sensors), temporal PSNR/SSIM for visual quality, and frame latency to assess responsiveness.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior sampling approaches and adaptive rendering schemes, our method explicitly incorporates power-awareness and hierarchical temporal sampling tailored for time-gated rendering in mobile AR contexts, providing a quantitative framework for balancing energy and visual quality that adapts in real time to both scene dynamics and device power constraints.

IDEA: Develop a compact learned temporal encoding framework with aggressive model compression and lightweight decoding tailored for memory-constrained embedded IoT devices, enabling high-fidelity time-gated rendering with under 100 KB of memory usage.

BACKGROUND: Time-gated rendering improves image quality by exploiting temporal sampling of scene illumination, but current learned temporal encoding models require large memory footprints and computational resources unsuitable for embedded IoT platforms. Existing NeRF accelerators like ICARUS focus on performance for GPUs or specialized hardware but do not address extreme memory and latency constraints typical of low-cost IoT vision devices.

APPROACH: Design a temporal encoding network architecture optimized for extreme model compression using techniques such as quantization-aware training, structured pruning, and knowledge distillation to fit within <100 KB of memory. Couple this with a lightweight reconstruction pipeline employing efficient temporal feature interpolation and sparse decoding schemes, specifically tuned to time-gated input sequences. Implement and optimize the method on representative embedded platforms (e.g., ARM Cortex-M and NVIDIA Jetson Nano).

EXPERIMENT: Evaluate on publicly available time-gated imaging datasets such as the Time-of-Flight (ToF) Indoor Dataset and simulated NeRF temporal sequences. Metrics include PSNR and SSIM for reconstruction fidelity, model size in KB, and inference latency measured on embedded IoT hardware prototypes.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines extreme memory-aware learned temporal encoding with reconstruction tailored explicitly for time-gated rendering on severely resource-limited embedded devices, overcoming the gap left by prior GPU-focused NeRF accelerators and large-memory learned models.

IDEA: Develop a memory-constrained epigenetic reprogramming protocol targeting key iron homeostasis regulators in senescent cells to achieve stable normalization of iron metabolism post-transplantation with minimal molecular interventions.

BACKGROUND: Senescent cells accumulate iron, contributing to oxidative stress and altering ferroptosis susceptibility, which complicates cell-based therapies and transplantation outcomes. Existing approaches involve broad molecular editing or extensive reprogramming, risking off-target effects and phenotype reversion. There is a critical need for precise, minimal epigenetic interventions that sustain iron homeostasis in senescent cells long-term after transplantation.

APPROACH: We propose to identify and selectively epigenetically modulate a minimal set of regulatory loci (such as promoters/enhancers of TFR1, ferritin, and key iron exporters) via CRISPR-dCas9-based epigenetic editors (e.g., dCas9-TET1 or dCas9-KRAB) to reset iron handling gene expression profiles in senescent cells. This “memory-constrained” reprogramming will be designed to avoid large-scale chromatin remodeling and focus on durable, targeted DNA methylation or histone modification changes. Ex vivo reprogrammed senescent cells will then be transplanted into murine models to assess maintenance of iron homeostasis and senescence phenotype stability.

EXPERIMENT: Validate using doxorubicin-induced senescent human fibroblasts with characterized iron overload; measure iron-related gene expression and epigenetic marks (ChIP-seq for histone mods, bisulfite sequencing for DNA methylation) pre- and post-reprogramming, and longitudinally post-transplant in NSG mice. Assess intracellular iron levels (e.g., calcein-AM assay), lipid peroxidation (BODIPY-C11), and ferroptosis susceptibility. Compare against non-reprogrammed and extensively reprogrammed controls, using metrics of iron homeostasis stability and senescence marker retention.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing on broad genetic or pharmacological intervention, this approach employs precision, minimal epigenetic editing to achieve durable iron regulation with reduced off-target risks and molecular complexity, enabling practical and safer transplantation of senescent cells with sustained iron homeostasis.

IDEA: Develop and validate a memory-constrained nanoparticle platform for selective delivery of iron chelators to senescent cells in aged organs, optimizing for minimal size and payload complexity to enhance targeting specificity and repeat dosing capability.

BACKGROUND: Senescent cells in aged tissues accumulate iron, contributing to oxidative stress and dysfunction, yet current iron chelation strategies lack targeted delivery and often involve bulky carriers that limit tissue penetration and dosing frequency. Efficient selective targeting of senescent cells to reduce iron overload without triggering immune responses remains an unmet need for improving aged organ function and mitigating iron-driven senescence pathologies.

APPROACH: Engineer ultrasmall nanoparticles (~20-50 nm) conjugated with senescence-associated beta-galactosidase (SA-β-gal)-responsive ligands to selectively release iron chelators intracellularly in senescent cells. The design minimizes carrier and payload memory footprint by employing modular minimalistic polymers and optimized drug loading, enabling repeated dosing with reduced immunogenicity and improved biodistribution in heterogeneous aged microenvironments.

EXPERIMENT: Evaluate selective uptake and iron-chelating efficacy using aged mouse models (e.g., 18-24 month C57BL/6) with established senescent cell markers; measure senescent cell iron content reduction via ICP-MS and ferroptosis markers by lipid peroxidation assays; track nanoparticle size distribution and payload retention with DLS and HPLC; benchmark against bulkier nanoparticle carriers and non-targeted chelation controls.

NOVELTY: This approach prioritizes an unprecedented minimal memory and size footprint in nanoparticle design for senescent cell targeting, advancing beyond existing bulky delivery systems by enabling higher targeting specificity, lower immunogenicity, and repeat dosing feasibility in aged organs, thus addressing a critical barrier in iron overload therapeutics for aging-related pathologies.

IDEA: Develop a latency-optimized iron chelation system that rapidly and selectively removes iron from circulating senescent cells in the bloodstream by leveraging ultra-fast binding chelators combined with flow-enhanced delivery and senescent cell surface marker targeting.

BACKGROUND: Senescent cells in the bloodstream exhibit iron overload that contributes to chronic inflammation and age-related pathologies, yet current iron chelation therapies lack the speed and selectivity needed to effectively and safely target these cells under physiological blood flow conditions. Existing approaches do not adequately balance rapid iron binding kinetics with selective uptake by senescent cells, leading to off-target iron depletion in normal blood components and systemic side effects.

APPROACH: Engineer a bifunctional iron chelator conjugated to ligands recognizing senescent cell-specific surface markers (e.g., β-galactosidase-induced epitopes or senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors), optimized for ultra-fast iron chelation kinetics. Employ microfluidic blood flow models to enhance chelator-target interactions ensuring rapid uptake and iron sequestration within senescent cells while minimizing interaction with normal erythrocytes or leukocytes. Validate delivery and chelation efficiency via real-time flow cytometry and iron-sensitive fluorescent probes.

EXPERIMENT: Use freshly isolated human peripheral blood samples spiked with doxorubicin-induced senescent lymphocytes as mimetics, measuring iron chelation kinetics via fluorescent iron probes and senescence markers through flow cytometry under dynamic flow conditions mimicking physiological shear stress. Evaluate systemic iron levels and off-target binding in controls lacking senescent cells, using serum ferritin and transferrin saturation assays as metrics.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior iron chelation therapies that focus on static conditions or systemic delivery, this approach uniquely integrates rapid-binding chelators with targeted delivery under flow, achieving selective iron removal from circulating senescent cells in real time, thus minimizing systemic iron depletion and potential adverse effects.

IDEA: Conduct a large-scale cross-linguistic psycholinguistic investigation into how speakers of typologically diverse languages interpret conditional perfection and its inferred causal meanings, isolating universal versus language-specific syntactic and semantic cues.

BACKGROUND: Conditional perfection—where a conditional “If p, then q” is pragmatically strengthened to “If and only if p, then q”—varies widely across languages, yet existing research offers limited empirical data beyond English and closely related languages. Moreover, the connection between conditional perfection and causal inference remains underexplored cross-linguistically, especially regarding how languages encode or allow causal implications from conditionals, creating a gap in understanding universal versus language-specific cognitive mechanisms.

APPROACH: Develop a standardized psycholinguistic experimental paradigm involving truth-value judgment and reaction time tasks with controlled conditional statements, tailored to the syntactic and semantic properties of each target language. Recruit native speakers from typologically diverse languages (e.g., Japanese, Turkish, Hindi, Finnish, and Zulu) to test how conditional perfection arises and interacts with causal inference cues, controlling for lexical causatives and modality. Analyze patterns using mixed-effects regression to isolate linguistic and cognitive factors influencing conditional perfection processing.

EXPERIMENT: Collect new experimental data from at least 5 typologically distinct languages, each with 50+ native speakers performing online truth-value judgment tasks and reaction time measurements on conditionals designed to elicit conditional perfection. Evaluate inference patterns, reaction times, and error rates, comparing across languages and correlating with syntactic/semantic features coded from linguistic descriptions.

NOVELTY: This study is the first to systematically combine cross-linguistic psycholinguistic experimentation with fine-grained semantic and syntactic analysis of conditional perfection and its causal effects, moving beyond English-centric theories to uncover universal cognitive mechanisms and language-specific variations in conditional inference and causation.

IDEA: Develop a probabilistic, real-time model for recognizing conditional perfection in noisy, spontaneous spoken dialogue that dynamically resolves ambiguity and incomplete conditionals by leveraging discourse context and speech disfluency patterns.

BACKGROUND: Conditional perfection—where conditional statements (“If P, Q”) are interpreted as biconditional (“P if and only if Q”)—is well-studied in controlled text, but recognizing it in natural, noisy spoken dialogue remains an open problem due to incomplete utterances, disfluencies, and ambiguous phrasing. Existing semantic frameworks assume idealized conditions and fail to robustly interpret conditionals typical in spontaneous speech, limiting applications in dialogue systems and conversational AI.

APPROACH: We propose a Bayesian graphical model integrating acoustic-prosodic cues, partial syntactic parses, and discourse context to probabilistically infer conditional perfection in real time. The model incorporates a tailored spoken dialogue corpus annotated for conditional perfection phenomena and disfluency markers, using hidden states representing potential conditional interpretations and updating beliefs with incremental speech input and conversational signals.

EXPERIMENT: Evaluate on the Switchboard corpus augmented with targeted annotations for conditionals and disfluencies, comparing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 scores against baselines including deterministic semantic parsers and static rule-based conditional perfection detectors. Perform ablation studies to assess the contribution of prosodic and discourse features.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior static or text-bound models, this approach explicitly handles incomplete and ambiguous conditionals typical of noisy spoken dialogue by combining linguistic, prosodic, and contextual information within a probabilistic framework, enabling robust and incremental recognition of conditional perfection in real-time conversational settings.

text:
IDEA: Design and implement controlled, language-neutral cognitive experiments to isolate universal processing mechanisms underlying conditional perfection and its relation to causal inference across typologically diverse languages.

BACKGROUND: Conditional perfection (CP) occurs when a conditional ("if P then Q") is inferred to mean a biconditional ("if and only if P then Q"), yet its cognitive origins and relationship to causal reasoning remain debated, especially given potential confounds from language-specific forms and pragmatics. Prior cross-linguistic studies often conflate typological differences with cognitive universals, leaving open whether CP effects derive from universal causal cognition or language-specific cues.

APPROACH: Develop non-verbal, task-based experiments that present participants from diverse linguistic backgrounds with conditional scenarios represented via minimal, abstract stimuli (e.g., visual symbol sequences or interactive causal animations) to elicit and measure conditional perfection and causal inference without reliance on language-specific structures. Compare behavioral responses (e.g., choice patterns, reaction times) to systematically manipulate conditional form and causal context, isolating universal cognitive signatures of CP.

EXPERIMENT: Recruit speakers of typologically diverse languages with varied conditional marking (e.g., English, Japanese, Turkish, and a non-Indo-European language), administer the designed controlled tasks using an online platform, and evaluate convergence in CP rates and causal inference metrics (e.g., forced-choice endorsement, response latency). Baselines include standard language-based conditional judgment tasks from prior literature.

NOVELTY: By minimizing linguistic form variance through abstract, cross-linguistically neutral experimental designs, this research disentangles universal cognitive mechanisms underpinning conditional perfection from language-specific pragmatic or grammatical influences—advancing beyond prior cross-linguistic work that relied on natural language stimuli and thus conflated typological and cognitive factors.

IDEA: Develop a minimally invasive, high-resolution fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based imaging protocol to dynamically map cellular prion protein (PrP<sup>C</sup>) interactions and conformational changes in live mouse brain slices under physiological conditions.

BACKGROUND: Current understanding of prion propagation is limited by static or fixed-tissue approaches that fail to capture the transient and dynamic molecular interactions driving prion conversion and spread in intact neural circuits. Most studies rely on endpoint biochemical assays or fixed histology, lacking temporal resolution and physiological context to elucidate how PrP<sup>C</sup> interactions evolve during early and late stages of prion disease progression.

APPROACH: We will engineer fluorescently tagged PrP<sup>C</sup> constructs optimized for FRET efficiency to report on proximity and conformational changes indicative of pathogenic conversion. Using acute live mouse brain slices from prion-infected and control animals, we will apply real-time two-photon microscopy combined with time-resolved FRET to capture spatial and temporal patterns of PrP<sup>C</sup> interactions at subcellular resolution. Imaging will be complemented by pharmacological manipulation of known modulators (e.g., plasmin treatment or tau fibril exposure) to assess effects on prion interaction dynamics.

EXPERIMENT: Experiments will utilize brain slices from well-characterized mouse models of prion disease (e.g., RML- or 263K-infected mice) at different disease stages. The imaging data will be quantitatively analyzed through FRET efficiency metrics and correlated with biochemical prion load assessed by proteinase K-resistant PrP<sup>Sc</sup> quantification. Reproducibility will be tested across key brain regions implicated in prion spread, such as hippocampus and thalamus.

NOVELTY: This approach enables direct, real-time visualization of prion protein interactions and conformational states in live neural tissue, capturing transient molecular events inaccessible to traditional fixed-sample or bulk biochemical methods. It bridges the gap between molecular prion biology and intact brain physiology, providing unprecedented insight into the spatiotemporal dynamics of prion propagation.

IDEA: Develop a memory-efficient sparse sampling framework to capture and reconstruct synthetic prion-like protein interactions in microfluidic neural circuit models, enabling extended high-resolution imaging without overwhelming onboard storage.

BACKGROUND: Understanding the dynamic propagation and interaction of prion proteins at single-cell resolution in microfluidic platforms is essential for elucidating cellular prion propagation mechanisms. However, continuous live imaging over prolonged periods generates massive datasets that exceed memory capabilities of microdevice systems, limiting temporal resolution or experiment duration. Existing studies lack solutions to balance detailed interaction mapping with hardware constraints inherent to these experimental setups.

APPROACH: Implement a compressed sensing-based sparse sampling strategy combined with adaptive temporal and spatial imaging schedules that selectively sample regions and times of high prion interaction activity within microfluidic neuron cultures seeded with synthetic prion mimics. The compressed data will be algorithmically reconstructed using known interaction priors and validated via ground-truth full-frame imaging subsets. Integration with onboard or near-device memory management will enable continuous, long-term observation without data overload.

EXPERIMENT: Use microfluidic platforms hosting cultured neurons exposed to fluorescently tagged synthetic prion aggregates; collect time-lapse imaging data comparing full-frame continuous capture versus sparse sampled data streams. Evaluate reconstruction quality with metrics such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM), and validate interaction network inference accuracy against full data baselines.

NOVELTY: This approach addresses a critical bottleneck in live-cell prion propagation studies by integrating memory-aware data acquisition with computational reconstruction, surpassing prior work limited by either hardware memory or reliance on complete data capture, thus enabling previously infeasible prolonged, high-resolution interaction mapping in microfluidic neural models.

IDEA: Develop a latency-optimized, automated high-throughput fluorescence assay for rapid screening of compounds that inhibit prion propagation in cultured cells by minimizing per-sample processing delay to accelerate hit identification.

BACKGROUND: Current high-throughput screens for prion propagation inhibitors focus primarily on maximizing throughput by parallelizing assays but often involve lengthy incubation times and complex processing steps that create bottlenecks in assay cycle time. Faster identification of modulatory compounds is hindered by these inherent delays, limiting screening efficiency and slowing drug discovery for prion diseases. Addressing assay latency directly could substantially speed up compound evaluation without sacrificing assay sensitivity.

APPROACH: Design and implement an automated fluorescence-based cell culture assay using immortalized prion-infected neuroblastoma cells engineered to report prion propagation via a fluorescent reporter linked to misfolded prion protein accumulation. Optimize assay conditions—including incubation time, reagent delivery, and fluorescence measurement—to minimize latency per well. Integrate robotic liquid handling and real-time fluorescence plate readers to enable continuous and rapid processing of samples with minimal manual intervention.

EXPERIMENT: Benchmark the latency-optimized assay against a conventional 96-well plate prion propagation assay using a library of known prion inhibitors and negative controls. Measure metrics such as total assay cycle time, per-sample latency, hit discovery rate, Z’-factor for assay robustness, and reproducibility. Validate hits by secondary assays of prion infectivity reduction in cell lysates.

NOVELTY: Unlike previous methods that emphasize solely increasing throughput via parallelization, this approach uniquely targets and optimizes assay latency at each step of the workflow, enabling faster turnaround per sample and accelerating the overall screening timeline for prion modulation compounds. This latency-centric strategy has not been systematically applied to prion propagation assays before.

IDEA: Develop a stability-guided mutational design framework for epoxide hydrolase variants that maintain high catalytic efficiency and resist substrate inhibition under industrial-scale high substrate concentrations.

BACKGROUND: Industrial biocatalysis requires enzymes that perform efficiently at high substrate loads, but epoxide hydrolases often suffer from substrate inhibition and reduced stability under such conditions. Existing enzyme engineering efforts largely focus on maximizing catalytic activity alone, neglecting the balance between stability and performance at elevated substrate concentrations, limiting their practical application.

APPROACH: Integrate mechanistic insights from substrate binding and turnover with computational stability prediction tools (e.g., FoldX, Rosetta) to screen and prioritize mutations expected to enhance enzyme robustness without compromising catalytic function. This includes targeted mutagenesis of active site and distal residues influencing substrate inhibition and structural integrity, followed by iterative in vitro validation under simulated industrial conditions.

EXPERIMENT: Construct a library of designed mutants expressed and purified for kinetic characterization measuring parameters such as k_cat, K_M, and substrate inhibition constants (K_i) using model substrates (e.g., cis-epoxysuccinate). Evaluate thermal and operational stability via differential scanning fluorimetry and continuous batch reactions at high substrate concentrations; benchmark against wild-type and high-activity-only mutants.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focused solely on catalytic turnover or inhibition mechanisms, this approach systematically balances catalytic efficiency with enzyme stability and substrate inhibition resilience under industrially relevant conditions, enabling more practical and robust epoxide hydrolases for biocatalytic applications.

IDEA: Develop a memory-efficient hierarchical QM/MM simulation framework integrated with mesoscale membrane models to accurately and efficiently characterize the catalytic mechanism of membrane-associated epoxide hydrolases.

BACKGROUND: Epoxide hydrolases (EHs) associated with biological membranes catalyze epoxide ring opening with significant biomedical and industrial importance, but their catalytic mechanisms remain incompletely understood due to the complexity of membrane-enzyme-substrate interactions. Conventional QM/MM simulations capturing detailed catalytic chemistry at membrane interfaces require prohibitively high computational memory and resources, limiting exploration of long timescale dynamics and diverse membrane environments.

APPROACH: We propose coupling a reduced-memory QM/MM engine that employs localized basis sets and dynamic resolution adaptation with coarse-grained mesoscale membrane models that preserve essential lipid-protein interactions. This hierarchical multiscale framework enables focused quantum treatment of the catalytic site while embedding it in a realistic membrane environment represented by mesoscale simulations, facilitating efficient long-timescale sampling of enzyme catalysis and substrate binding/release pathways.

EXPERIMENT: Validation will be performed on well-characterized membrane-associated EHs such as human microsomal epoxide hydrolase (mEH) and bacterial cis-epoxysuccinate hydrolase using established benchmark substrates. Catalytic rates, reaction energy barriers, and intermediate states will be compared against experimental kinetic data and prior full QM/MM studies, while memory usage metrics will quantify computational savings.

NOVELTY: This method uniquely integrates adaptive memory-aware QM/MM algorithms with mesoscale membrane modeling, enabling unprecedented simulation efficiency without sacrificing mechanistic accuracy, overcoming the major bottleneck of standard QM/MM membrane simulations. This expands the feasible scope for in silico studies of EH catalysis in physiologically relevant membrane contexts.

IDEA: Genetically encode site-specific mechanistic probes via unnatural amino acid incorporation into epoxide hydrolase variants expressed in living cells to enable real-time, minimally invasive monitoring of catalytic activity and mechanism under native conditions.

BACKGROUND: Understanding epoxide hydrolase catalytic mechanisms in vivo remains challenging due to the lack of minimally disruptive tools that directly report on enzyme function within cells. Existing probes or inhibitors often perturb cellular metabolism or fail to provide dynamic mechanistic insight, limiting our ability to correlate structure-function relationships under physiological conditions. There is a need for a genetically encoded system that enables precise, real-time monitoring of epoxide hydrolase catalysis without compromising cellular health or enzyme activity.

APPROACH: Engineer epoxide hydrolase variants incorporating unnatural amino acids bearing environment-sensitive fluorescent or spectroscopic probes at mechanistically relevant active site residues using optimized amber suppression technology. Screen multiple probe sites to identify placements that preserve native catalytic function and demonstrate fluorescence or other readout changes upon substrate binding or turnover. Express these variants in model microbial or mammalian cell lines under controlled conditions to enable in-cell catalysis monitoring via live-cell fluorescence microscopy or time-resolved spectroscopy.

EXPERIMENT: Validate catalytic activity of engineered enzyme variants through in vitro kinetic assays (k_cat, K_M) compared to wild-type controls; confirm probe signal responsiveness to substrate presence and reaction progression in purified and cellular contexts. Assess cellular health markers (viability, proliferation, metabolic activity) post-expression. Benchmark dynamic in-cell readouts against traditional biochemical assays and mass spectrometry-based product quantification for correlation accuracy.

NOVELTY: This approach uniquely integrates genetic code expansion with mechanistic probe design targeted specifically to epoxide hydrolases, enabling minimally perturbative, real-time catalytic monitoring directly inside living cells—a capability not achieved by prior static or inhibitor-based methods. It advances mechanistic enzymology by bridging in vitro insights with physiological enzyme behavior.

IDEA: Develop a dynamic computational framework to model temporal variations in mechanical stress at tricellular junctions during epithelial morphogenesis, integrating evolving tissue geometry and protein distribution data.

BACKGROUND: While static analyses of mechanical stress at tricellular junctions (TCJs) provide insights into their role in orienting cell division and tissue mechanics, they fail to capture transient mechanotransduction events and the dynamic remodeling during development. Existing models lack the ability to simulate how forces at TCJs fluctuate in time alongside morphogenetic progression and changing protein compositions, limiting understanding of their regulatory functions during embryogenesis.

APPROACH: Construct a time-resolved biomechanical model coupling vertex-based tissue mechanics with dynamic biochemical fields representing key junctional proteins (e.g., E-cadherin, actomyosin) at TCJs. Incorporate live imaging-derived tissue geometry and fluorescently tagged protein expression as inputs to simulate evolving mechanical stresses and feedback over developmental time. Use finite element or agent-based simulations to predict force trajectories at TCJs during Drosophila wing disc morphogenesis.

EXPERIMENT: Validate the model against high-resolution live imaging datasets of Drosophila wing disc epithelia expressing TCJ force sensors (e.g., Vinculin tension sensor) and protein reporters, comparing simulated and measured junctional tension dynamics via correlation metrics and spatiotemporal pattern matching.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior static or shape-based analyses, this approach explicitly models the temporal evolution of mechanical stresses at TCJs in coordination with biochemical signaling and tissue remodeling, enabling the capture of transient mechanotransduction events and a mechanistic understanding of TCJ function during morphogenesis.

IDEA: Develop a stochastic computational model of tricellular junction (TCJ) mechanics that incorporates cancer-induced heterogeneity in junctional composition and mechanical degradation to predict tissue-level mechanical responses during tumor invasion.

BACKGROUND: While mechanical stress at TCJs is known to influence epithelial tissue integrity and mitotic orientation, existing models typically assume homogeneous junctional properties observed in healthy tissue. Cancer progression disrupts junctional proteins and introduces spatial heterogeneity, leading to stochastic variations in mechanical properties that are not well characterized or modeled, limiting our understanding of mechanical failure and invasion pathways at TCJs.

APPROACH: Construct a probabilistic framework that treats TCJ mechanical parameters (e.g., stiffness, adhesion strength) as random variables with distributions inferred from experimental data on tumor-adjacent epithelia. The model will simulate junctional degradation events and mechanical fluctuations at single TCJs, then upscale to predict stress distributions and failure probabilities at the tissue scale. Parameter estimation will incorporate atomic force microscopy (AFM) and traction force microscopy (TFM) data from cancerous and adjacent normal epithelial samples.

EXPERIMENT: Validate the model using published and newly acquired datasets that measure local forces and junctional protein expression at TCJs in tumor-adjacent human epithelial biopsies, evaluating predictive accuracy with metrics such as root mean square error (RMSE) between simulated and observed force distributions and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves for junction failure prediction.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely integrates stochastic heterogeneity of TCJ mechanical behavior induced by cancer with spatially resolved experimental data, moving beyond deterministic and homogeneous models to capture the unpredictable nature of junctional mechanics during tumor invasion, thereby providing a mechanistic tool to link molecular heterogeneity with emergent mechanical dysfunction.

IDEA: Develop a multi-scale computational model that integrates tricellular junction (TCJ) mechanics with dynamic extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling to investigate how altered matrix stiffness feedback modulates TCJ stress and epithelial tissue behavior in fibrotic disease.

BACKGROUND: While TCJs critically influence epithelial mechanics and organization, current models primarily consider cell-intrinsic factors without capturing the feedback from ECM changes under pathological conditions such as fibrosis. Fibrotic tissues exhibit increased ECM stiffness and abnormal remodeling, which likely alter local stresses at TCJs, but quantitative frameworks linking these scales remain lacking. Understanding this coupling is essential to elucidate how matrix mechanics drive altered cell junction forces and tissue dysfunction.

APPROACH: Build a multi-scale computational framework coupling a vertex-based epithelial tissue model that explicitly represents TCJs with a continuum description of ECM remodeling and stiffening governed by biochemical and biomechanical cues. The model will incorporate feedback loops wherein ECM stiffness modulates junctional tension and, conversely, junctional forces influence ECM remodeling rates. Parameterization will be informed by experimental measurements of TCJ protein localization and ECM composition from fibrotic versus healthy human tissue samples.

EXPERIMENT: Validate the model by comparing simulated mechanical stress distributions at TCJs with immunofluorescence staining of TCJ proteins (e.g., tricellulin, ZO-1) and atomic force microscopy-derived stiffness maps of fibrotic human lung biopsy samples. Evaluate predictive power by correlating junctional stress changes with ECM remodeling markers and cell proliferation rates under varying matrix stiffness conditions.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing solely on epithelial cell shape or intrinsic mechanical forces, this approach explicitly models the bidirectional coupling between TCJs and ECM remodeling in disease contexts, providing mechanistic insight into how pathological matrix stiffening alters epithelial junction mechanics and tissue function at multiple scales.
